headline: High-risk shared-write and MCP-enabled interaction: AutoGen can write local workspaces while Haystack can consume MCP/REST inputs, creating default-path prompt, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and uses stdin/stdout tool calls; Haystack can consume MCP servers and REST APIs. If AutoGen outputs are routed into Haystack via shared files or MCP, attacker-controlled content can be treated as instructions. The pairwise bridge is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF AutoGen writes untrusted content into a shared workspace that Haystack reads
IF Haystack ingests MCP or REST payloads from AutoGen without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP ingestion for untrusted sources
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages
Require human review before executing file-derived instructions

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen explicitly handles model provider API keys and can read/write files in configured working directories; Haystack has broad network egress and can call REST/MCP endpoints. If both touch the same workspace, sensitive application data can flow from AutoGen into Haystack outputs or outbound requests. The shared-workspace pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same filesystem workspace
IF Haystack forwards retrieved file contents or prompts to external APIs
mitigations: Use separate directories and credentials
Redact secrets before handoff
Restrict Haystack outbound destinations
Turn off file ingestion for sensitive folders
Rotate any exposed API keys

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen has shell, subprocess, package-install, and filesystem-write capabilities; Haystack has broad network egress and MCP/REST access. Their mutable surfaces overlap on shared files and external calls, so concurrent writes or conflicting side effects are plausible even though AutoGen does not modify git state. No locking is documented, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same writable directory
IF Haystack and AutoGen are allowed to mutate the same external resource without locks
mitigations: Assign disjoint writable paths
Serialize access with a simple lock file
Disable package installs during shared runs
Scope each agent to separate API credentials
Snapshot state before concurrent execution

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool outputs and code-execution results; Haystack is a search/RAG system that can consume those outputs as inputs. If Haystack treats AutoGen output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream retrieval, summaries, or actions. Because the verification step is not documented, the default-path risk is high.
conditions: IF Haystack uses AutoGen-generated text as retrieval context or final answer material
IF no verification or citation-check step is inserted between agents
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require source citations for every claim
Compare outputs against original documents
Limit Haystack to summarization only
Flag low-confidence AutoGen outputs for review

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not declare regulated-data certifications or residency constraints. AutoGen touches application data and model-provider API keys, while Haystack only lists anonymous usage statistics. No specific residency or retention mismatch is evidenced, so compliance risk is limited to documented gaps rather than a clear violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through either agent without a separate policy review
IF retention or residency settings differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Document retention settings for both agents
Confirm deployment region for each service
Review logging defaults
Add a data-classification gate before handoff
